chapter.name: Probability
chapter.blurb: The classical (theoretical) definition of probability, P(E) = favourable outcomes over total outcomes for equally likely outcomes, replacing the experimental probability of Class IX; the complementary-events rule P(E) + P(not E) = 1; the boundary cases of an impossible event (P=0) and a sure event (P=1) within 0 <= P(E) <= 1; probability with single draws from coins, dice, cards and everyday collections of objects; and compound experiments -- two or three coins tossed together, and two dice thrown together -- solved by listing every equally likely outcome rather than guessing. The chapter's own text also raises geometric (continuous-sample-space) probability through a musical-chair timing example and a helicopter-crash area, but explicitly marks both 'Not from the examination point of view', so this book's examinable content stops at finite, equally-likely sample spaces.

concepts.name: Theoretical (classical) probability: definition and equally likely outcomes
concepts.description: The theoretical (classical) probability of an event E, written P(E), is defined as P(E) = number of outcomes favourable to E / number of all possible outcomes of the experiment, valid only when the outcomes are equally likely; contrasted with the experimental/empirical probability (studied in Class IX) based on the results of actually repeating a trial.
concepts.idea: Instead of repeating an experiment many times and counting what actually happened (empirical probability), if every outcome is equally likely you can predict the probability in advance just by counting how many outcomes are favourable out of all possible outcomes.
concepts.rule: P(E) = Number of outcomes favourable to E / Number of all possible outcomes of the experiment, where the outcomes of the experiment are assumed equally likely. This is also called classical probability, given by Pierre Simon Laplace in 1795.
concepts.example: Tossing a fair coin once: the two outcomes head and tail are equally likely, so P(head) = 1/2 and P(tail) = 1/2 (pp. 202-204).

concepts.name: Elementary events and finding P(E) for simple single-trial experiments
concepts.description: An elementary event is an event with exactly one outcome of the experiment; the sum of the probabilities of all the elementary events of an experiment is 1. Applying the theoretical probability definition to single draws from coins, dice, and collections of distinguishable objects (balls, marbles, candies, coins, fish, discs, pens, bulbs, people).
concepts.idea: Break an experiment into its individual elementary outcomes; each one's probability is 1 over the total count, and grouping several elementary outcomes into one named event just adds their probabilities.
concepts.rule: An event with only one outcome is an elementary event. If an experiment has n equally likely elementary outcomes, each has probability 1/n, and the sum of the probabilities of all n elementary events is n x (1/n) = 1. For an event E with k favourable outcomes among n, P(E) = k/n.
concepts.example: A box has 3 blue, 2 white and 4 red marbles (9 total); P(white) = 2/9, P(blue) = 3/9 = 1/3, P(red) = 4/9, and 2/9 + 3/9 + 4/9 = 1 (Example 8, p. 209).

concepts.name: The range of probability: impossible events, sure events, and 0 <= P(E) <= 1
concepts.description: For any event E, 0 <= P(E) <= 1. An event that has no favourable outcome (P(E) = 0) is an impossible event; an event where every outcome is favourable (P(E) = 1) is a sure or certain event.
concepts.idea: The favourable-outcome count can never be negative and never exceeds the total, so probability is pinned between 0 (can't happen) and 1 (must happen), with everything else in between.
concepts.rule: For any event E, 0 <= P(E) <= 1. P(E) = 0 exactly when E is impossible (no outcome favours it). P(E) = 1 exactly when E is sure/certain (every outcome favours it).
concepts.example: For a single die thrown once, P(getting 8) = 0/6 = 0 (impossible, no face shows 8); P(getting a number less than 7) = 6/6 = 1 (sure, every face qualifies) (pp. 206-207).

concepts.name: Compound experiments: two dice, the 36-outcome sample space, and sums
concepts.description: When two dice are thrown together (or one die is thrown twice), the possible outcomes are the 36 ordered pairs (first die, second die), each equally likely; events are often described in terms of the sum of the two numbers, or in terms of a value appearing (or not appearing) on either die.
concepts.idea: Lay the 36 outcomes out as a 6-by-6 table, first die's number down the side and second die's number across the top, so that counting favourable outcomes for any 'sum' or 'appears on either die' event becomes a matter of reading cells off the table rather than guessing.
concepts.rule: Two dice give 36 equally likely ordered-pair outcomes (i,j), i,j from 1 to 6, since (1,4) and (4,1) are different outcomes. For a sum s, count the ordered pairs adding to s directly from the table. For 'a value v does not appear on either die', count pairs using only the other 5 numbers on each die: 5x5 = 25 outcomes.
concepts.example: Two dice thrown together: P(sum = 8) = 5/36, using the 5 pairs (2,6),(3,5),(4,4),(5,3),(6,2) (Example 13, pp. 212-213). A die thrown twice: P(5 does not come up either time) = 25/36, so P(5 comes up at least once) = 1 - 25/36 = 11/36 (Exercise 14.1, Q24, p. 216).

questions.q: A student argues: 'When two dice are thrown, the possible sums are 2, 3, 4, ..., 12 -- that is 11 different sums. So each sum has probability 1/11.' (i) State how many of the 36 equally likely outcomes give a sum of 2, and how many give a sum of 7. (ii) Using your answer to (i), find P(sum = 2) and P(sum = 7). (iii) Explain clearly why the student's reasoning is incorrect.
questions.a: (i) Sum of 2: only (1,1), so 1 outcome. Sum of 7: (1,6),(2,5),(3,4),(4,3),(5,2),(6,1), so 6 outcomes. (ii) P(sum=2) = 1/36. P(sum=7) = 6/36 = 1/6. (iii) The student's reasoning is incorrect because the 11 possible sums are not equally likely outcomes of the experiment -- the actual 36 equally likely outcomes are the ordered pairs (i,j), and different sums are made up of different numbers of these pairs (only 1 pair gives a sum of 2, but 6 pairs give a sum of 7), so the 11 sums cannot each have the same probability 1/11.

questions.q: A classmate says: 'Since a single die thrown once has 6 equally likely outcomes, throwing it twice should have 6+6=12 equally likely outcomes.' Evaluate this claim.
questions.a: The claim is false. Throwing a die twice (or throwing two dice together) has 6 x 6 = 36 equally likely outcomes, not 6 + 6 = 12 -- each of the 6 outcomes of the first throw can be paired with each of the 6 outcomes of the second throw, which is multiplication, not addition, of the two counts.
s: States the claim is false
Explains the correct reasoning: outcomes multiply (6x6=36), not add
